member.name: T:GetAndSee.Core.Device.AbandonableReadStream
member.summary: Read-only decorator that shields the copy loop from an orphaned device read so the run-level can stop a stuck transfer cleanly (#11 / #25 / #42 / R2).

remarks.para: The native AFC read is a blocking call with no timeout, dispatched onto a thread-pool worker. A cable yank, a sleeping device, or a USB bus reset can make it park forever or pin a core and never return. This decorator races each against the supplied cancellation token: when the run-level forward-progress watchdog observes that bytes have stopped flowing and trips that token, the in-flight read is abandoned and an is surfaced, so the caller is never blocked on the orphaned read.

Unlike the Sprint 2 design, this decorator no longer owns its own inactivity timer. Liveness is a single run-level concept driven by the byte heartbeat; this type only provides the two things the watchdog needs to act on a stuck read: (1) an abandon-on-cancellation race so a cancel actually unblocks the pinned read, and (2) a private reusable scratch buffer so an abandoned read that keeps writing can never corrupt a pooled buffer already handed back to the caller's .

On abandonment, disposal of the inner stream (which closes the native AFC handle) is scheduled for whenever the orphaned read eventually returns or faults — so the handle is not leaked. If the read never returns, the process is exiting anyway and the OS reclaims it.

member.name: T:GetAndSee.Core.Device.DeviceWatchdog
member.summary: The shared device-inactivity watchdog: races a blocking device operation against a timeout on an injectable and, if the operation does not settle in time, abandons it and throws so the run can stop cleanly and resumably (#11 / #25 / R2).

remarks.para: The native AFC calls (afc_file_open, afc_read_directory, afc_get_file_info, afc_file_read) are blocking with no timeout: a cable yank, a sleeping device, or a USB bus reset parks them forever (the #11/#25 hang). This helper runs the operation off the caller's path and races it against . If the timeout wins, the operation is abandoned: a continuation is scheduled so that whenever it eventually settles, any resource it produced is released (no handle leak), while the caller gets a instead of blocking forever.

This is the single implementation of the abandon-on-timeout/abandon-on-cancellation logic. The four blocking native calls (open/stat/list) guard against a parked call with a timeout here, and reuses the same race to abandon a stuck read when the run-level forward-progress watchdog cancels it — so the behavior is defined and tested in exactly one place.

member.name: T:GetAndSee.Core.Organize.DateFolderOrganizer
member.summary: Maps a remote file to its relative destination path under a chosen when a sane capture date is available, otherwise unsorted/<name>.

member.name: T:GetAndSee.Core.Reorganize.Reorganizer
member.summary: Migrates an existing archive to a different by moving files within the archive root only — an offline, atomic, resumable operation (the first thing in the product that moves files on the PC). Data integrity is sacred: every move is a same-volume atomic rename followed by a single journal update, a crash between the two is reconciled on the next run, and no file is ever lost, truncated, or clobbered.

remarks.para: Flow (see ):

list.item: write the in-flight reorganize_target marker so an interruption is detectable and resumable;
for each planned move, in the deterministic plan order: ensure the target folder, atomic , then ;
crash-reconcile — a file already at its target (source gone, size matches) heals the journal; a file missing from both places is a per-file failure that never drops the row;
on a fully clean run (no per-file failures), stamp the new scheme and clear the marker.

remarks.para: Offline: the reorganizer has no device dependency — it never references IPhoneClient or makes any AFC/lockdown call. It reads placement inputs from the journal only, so the read-only device contract is untouched.

Collision determinism: new collisions (a coarser layout mapping two files to one target) are resolved with the shared _2/_3 rule against the in-run assignment set only — never on-disk existence. A resumed run therefore re-derives the exact same suffixed target a prior run assigned; a file physically moved to that target but not yet journaled is healed at move time rather than bumped again. Clobber-safety is enforced at move time by the non-overwrite plus a size-checked reconcile.

member.name: T:GetAndSee.Core.Transfer.DisconnectEscapeHatch
member.summary: The Sprint 3.4 disconnect escape-hatch: the single action run on the forward-progress watchdog's independent timer thread when the device is proven gone (#45). It writes the run summary and terminates the process with exit code 3 without unwinding through native device code.

remarks.para: Five rounds of guarding individual native calls (read, open, stat, list) each relocated the hang to the next unguarded synchronous native call. #45 captured the real class live: on a mid-copy yank afc_file_read returns EmptyResponse/0 and the fault unwinds into the read stream's await using disposal → afc_file_close, which busy-spins forever on the dead transport.

When the byte heartbeat is dead the device is provably gone and the data is already safe (the journal is a crash-safe SQLite WAL with each file committed). So instead of trying to unwind gracefully through native code that may spin, this escape-hatch — running on the watchdog's independent timer thread, which the wedged main thread cannot block — prints the disconnect line, writes and flushes summary.txt from a fresh read-only journal connection (no device call), and hard-terminates the process via . The orphaned spinning native thread is reaped by the OS.

Summary writing is best-effort: the journal on disk is the durable source of truth and recovers on the next open, so a failure to refresh summary.txt must never prevent the terminate — the terminate is the load-bearing guarantee.

member.name: T:GetAndSee.Core.Transfer.ForwardProgressWatchdog
member.summary: The run-level forward-progress (liveness) watchdog: the single, manifestation-agnostic guard that turns "the device stopped delivering bytes" into a clean, resumable stop, regardless of why the bytes stopped (#11 → #25 → #38 → #42).

remarks.para: Every prior unplug fix guarded a specific code location (a parked read, a parked open, a between-file failure burst), and real hardware then found the next location. The one invariant across all of them is that forward byte progress stops — the staging .partial freezes. This watchdog watches that symptom directly via the existing per-chunk heartbeat (onBytesStreamed), on an independent timer that does not depend on any device read returning. While a copy is in flight, if no progress is recorded for timeout, it trips a single that the copy loop observes, unwinding to the existing / exit-3 path (resumable; summary.txt written).

It folds in the Sprint 3.2 forward-progress breaker (#38): a burst of consecutive per-file failures with no intervening progress (a cable-yank that fast-fails every file instead of parking) trips it immediately rather than waiting out the inactivity timer, so the journal is not churned through thousands of failed rows. A single success or any streamed byte resets the streak, so an isolated bad or changed file never trips it.

Why a run-level timer and not the old per-read inactivity timer: the per-read guard only armed when a read failed to complete promptly and was enforced through a thread-pool-scheduled continuation, so it provided no run-level, read-independent liveness — a read that returned fast-and-wrong, or a native read that pinned a core and never returned, slipped past it (the #42 intra-file spin). This guard is always armed while copying and fires on the heartbeat alone.
